rv.q: Nichols's satisfying production [gives] his staging of the play a particularly shocking subliminal punch. And Hoffman, an eloquent package of virulence and vulnerability, finds all the crazy music in Willy's disappointment. Gravity seems to hang on his lumpy body like a rumpled suit, tethering him to the shaky ground he stands on.
Every choice feels right, and every note of Miller's play sounds clear as a bell.
And the play, 63 years after it changed Miller's life and the theater, still holds the stage with the certainty of tires on tough cement.
Hoffman meets that challenge fiercely, dressed to perfect disadvantage.

The Great Recession is the unbilled star of Mike Nichols’ Broadway revival of Arthur Miller’s “Death of a Salesman” — the scene-stealing specter, invisible but ever-present, that gives the production its ferocious relevance more than 60 years after the play’s birth.
Too bad his name doesn’t sell tickets the way Hoffman’s does — and the audience gets the wrong end of the bargain.
Yet the tears that brimmed in my eyes in those initial wordless moments receded almost as soon as the first dialogue was spoken.
The gap between those two sets of reactions explains why “Salesman,” now and forever a great play, never quite achieves greatness on the stage this time around.
That Arthur Miller’s take on the deception of the American myth of success is the hottest ticket on Broadway is deservedly the case.
Mike Nichols's magnificent revival of Arthur Miller's 1949 epilogue for the American Dream
While this Salesman owes much to tradition, it pulses with energy and urgency.
Also remarkable is that we never really know what Willy sells — mostly, he tries to hawk himself to businesses, his family, himself.
Miller gives Death of a Salesman a muscular narrative arc, and this revival provides the intensity to flex it and strike.
"Under the direction of Mike Nichols, the production overall has an uneven, uninflected quality, without the dramatic solidity or shadings of personality that make a work spring to vivid life.
Nichols’ excellent company of actors seamlessly handles the classic’s demands, capably navigating the ebb and flow of time and emotion.
And director Mike Nichols has put together a cast that doesn’t quite come together.

cn.t: Mike Nichols' reverential revival earns strong praise for its emotional power and Philip Seymour Hoffman's nuanced performance, though some critics find the production uneven and Hoffman miscast as the iconic Willy Loman.

sg.ra: TickPick and Headout both name Center Orchestra rows E-J (TickPick: E-J; SeatPlan/Headout: F-O) as the prime zone at the Barrymore because the 1,058-seat house is shallow enough that the mezzanine overhang only kicks in at row K of the orchestra, leaving center rows F-J with an uncovered, forward sightline well-suited to the text-driven plays this house tends to book.

Headout and TickPick both warn against Orchestra rows A-C at the Barrymore specifically because the stage at this 1928 house sits high relative to the front rows — TickPick: 'rows A, B, and C are too close to the stage and might block your view'; Headout adds that 'seats closer to the stage may cause neck strain from looking upward.'

SeatPlan and TickPick both confirm the Barrymore mezzanine overhang begins at row K of the orchestra but isn't obstructive — SeatPlan: 'those sitting in the rear of the Orchestra section will notice that the stage feels impressively close'; the house's well-raked orchestra keeps sightlines intact even under cover, which matters because this is a 1,058-seat intimate-play house and losing the rear orchestra would shrink the good-seat pool significantly.

sg.vl: Elevated wide view, under premium pricing
sg.ra: SeatPlan directly names row A Center Front Mezzanine as the house favorite at the Barrymore — 'very popular thanks to its fantastic elevated position above the stage' — and both SeatPlan and TickPick emphasize the Barrymore's front mezzanine is only 5 rows deep (A-E, 196 seats), so even row E retains a wide, pitched view and benefits from the intimate 1,058-seat scale.

SeatPlan specifically praises the Barrymore rear mezzanine rake: 'a decent rake means even the back rows offer a surprisingly good look at the stage' and 'even in the far corner theatergoers won't feel too much strain to make out the stage.' The house's three-flights-up rear mezz is the trade-off for the small footprint, but the rake compensates for distance in a way deeper houses don't manage.

Headout and TickPick both flag the Barrymore's six box seats (three per side of the orchestra) and the orchestra rows D-E directly beneath them as compromised — Headout: 'seats under the Boxes in rows D and E a little restricted'; TickPick adds 'far Left and Right Orchestra and the outer corners of the Mezzanine can have reduced sightlines.' This is a specific quirk of the Barrymore's 1928 proscenium layout with built-in side boxes.
